#### Two views, one writer each — stack and heap at every step

**What is being answered.** How two views of one balance are kept consistent — and what the consistency check can and cannot catch.

`applyWrite` does both writes in one place: the table row, then a Record carrying `before` and the new value. One writer per view, so agreement is structural rather than maintained.

`audit` re-folds the log and compares totals. Step 4 runs it with one capture deliberately skipped: the table reads 45 and the re-folded log reads 37, so `agree` is false and the gap is exactly the uncaptured 8. Without that check it is a fraud feed silently missing a balance change.

The animation steps through the code, holding each line long enough to read the STACK (call frames and their locals) and the HEAP (allocated arrays and objects) as they are AT THAT MOMENT. Expand any step to study it on its own.

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch06-system-memory/ch06-system-memory.svg" alt="Two views, one writer each — stack and heap at every step, 4 steps showing stack and heap" width="980">

<details>
<summary><b>Step 1 of 4</b> — the application writes the table; CDC writes the log</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch06-system-memory/frames/step-01.svg" alt="Step 1: the application writes the table; CDC writes the log" width="980">

Two writes, one per view, and they are in the same function so they cannot get out of step: `tbl.rows` is updated, then a Record carrying `before` and the new value is appended. Nothing else in the design writes either view — which is what makes agreement structural rather than hoped for.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 of 4</b> — re-folding the log reconstructs the table</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch06-system-memory/frames/step-02.svg" alt="Step 2: re-folding the log reconstructs the table" width="980">

`tbl.rows[r.key] = r.new` — each record names the result, so the fold is an assignment rather than an accumulation. The derived table ends at "a" = 24, "b" = 21, which is exactly the real one. That is the derivation this design's guarantee rests on.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 of 4</b> — the audit compares the two, and agrees</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch06-system-memory/frames/step-03.svg" alt="Step 3: the audit compares the two, and agrees" width="980">

`totalOf(tbl)` = 45 and `totalOf(derived)` = 45, so `agree` is true. This is cheap enough to run continuously, and it is the only thing in the design that can fail loudly — which matters because the failure it catches is otherwise completely silent.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 4 of 4</b> — and one missed capture makes it disagree</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch06-system-memory/frames/step-04.svg" alt="Step 4: and one missed capture makes it disagree" width="980">

With `captureEvery` false the last write skips its Record, so the table reaches 45 and the re-folded log reaches 37. `agree` is false, and the gap is exactly the uncaptured 8. Without the audit this is a fraud feed quietly missing one balance change, and nothing else in the system notices.

</details>

<sub>Both audit outcomes are computed from the seed and asserted. Generated by `node tools/gen_ch06.js` on `tools/memkit.js`.</sub>
